title: But Yahweh Was with Him — Prospering, Running, Prison
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you all. Today I want to begin with a question, and the answer to this one question decides whether a great many people stay on their feet when trouble comes:
Does "God is with me" mean the same thing as "my affairs will go smoothly"?

A great many people understand it that way. So when the business collapses, when the body collapses, when a relationship collapses, the first thought is this: has God gone? Have I done something wrong somewhere?

In Genesis 39 there is one sentence that occurs four times: "Yahweh was with Joseph." And where those four occurrences fall is very interesting indeed — twice while he is a slave, and twice while he is in prison. Not one of the four falls in a season when life was going well.

"Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites that had brought him down there." (Genesis 39:1)

"Was brought down" is הוּרַד (*hurad*) in the Hebrew, a passive form. He did not go down; he was taken down. This is the life of a seventeen-year-old who had no say in a single thing that happened to him.
Then comes verse 2: "Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian."
Notice the order here. First comes "Yahweh was with Joseph", and only after that comes "he was a prosperous man." And what is he at this moment? A slave.
"Prosperous" is מַצְלִיחַ (*matzliach*), and this word occurs three times in the chapter. Psalm 1 says, "Whatever he does shall prosper" — that is this very word.
Brothers and sisters, how can a slave be "prosperous"? He has no freedom of person, no wages, no tomorrow. And yet the Bible says he prospered.
The prospering here is not the kind of prospering we talk about. What it means is this: the thing in his hands got done. In a place he wanted no part of whatsoever, he made the work come out right.
Verse 3 is more remarkable still: "His master saw that Yahweh was with him, and that Yahweh made all that he did prosper in his hand."

An idol-worshipping Egyptian could tell whose life Yahweh was in. He could not, of course, hear a word of what Joseph prayed. What he saw was the way this slave went about his work — on time, tidy, dependable, never idling, never shifting a responsibility onto somebody else.

Brothers and sisters, a great many people imagine that witness is a matter of the mouth. This verse tells us something different: when a person has God inside him, the quality of his work speaks on his behalf.

Verse 5: "From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. Yahweh's blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field."

"For Joseph's sake" — back in chapter 30 Laban said something very like it to Jacob. This is the promise of Genesis 12 still moving forward: "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you."
Where God's people are, that place comes under blessing. Not because we are especially outstanding, but because God is faithful.

And notice that expression, "in the house and in the field" — the blessing of Deuteronomy 28 is written in exactly that shape: "You shall be blessed in the city, and you shall be blessed in the field." Four hundred years before the law was ever given, that blessing had already come to rest on an Egyptian household that was being run by a slave.
"Yahweh was with Joseph" — is there something hidden in where that sentence falls?

The sentence occurs four times in this chapter, and the placing of those four is very interesting indeed: twice while he is a slave, twice while he is in prison, and not once in a season when life was going well. That single fact answers the question a great many people are carrying inside them — does "God is with me" mean the same thing as "my affairs will go smoothly"? The text's answer is this: his presence is not the same as an easy road; his presence means that in the place you want no part of, he is there. So when the business collapses, when the body collapses, when a relationship collapses, the first thought does not have to be "God has gone." God's presence is not measured by your circumstances. It is measured by what he has said.
How can a slave be a "prosperous man"?

Look at the order first. Verse 2 has "Yahweh was with Joseph" before it has "and he was a prosperous man" — and what he is at that moment is a slave, with no freedom of person, no wages and no tomorrow. So the prospering here is not the kind we talk about; what that word means is that the thing in his hands got done. In a place he wanted no part of whatsoever, he made the work come out right. That is a great comfort to a great many people sitting in a job they never wanted and in a family they never chose, and it is also a very practical direction: you cannot decide where you are put, but you can decide whether this one thing in your hands gets finished properly.
How could an idol-worshipping Egyptian "see that Yahweh was with him"?

Verse 3 puts it beautifully: the master could tell whose life Yahweh was in. He could not, of course, hear a word of what Joseph prayed. What he saw was the way this slave went about his work — on time, tidy, dependable, never idling, never shifting a responsibility onto somebody else. A great many people imagine that witness is a matter of the mouth; this verse tells us that when a person has God inside him, the quality of his work speaks on his behalf. For believers in the workplace this is the most practical road there is: rather than hurrying to find an opening to preach the gospel, first do the work so well that somebody wants to ask you, "Why are you different?" Doing it well is itself a kind of proclamation.
2. A Light from the Original: How Then Can I Do This Great Wickedness, and Sin Against God?
At the end of verse 6 a line is planted for what is coming: "Joseph was well-built and handsome."

In the original that phrase is יְפֵה־תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה (*yefeh to'ar vifeh mareh*), exactly the same wording used of Rachel in chapter 29. Very quietly, the text is telling us that trouble is about to break.
"After these things, his master's wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, 'Lie with me.'" (Genesis 39:7)

"Set her eyes on" is, in the Hebrew, "she lifted up her eyes towards him." In chapter 3, when Eve "saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes", it is that same kind of looking.
Joseph's answer is the beating heart of the whole chapter:

"But he refused, and said to his master's wife, 'Behold, my master doesn't know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand. No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?'" (Genesis 39:8–9)
Look at the three layers of his reasoning.
The first layer: my master trusts me. The very first thing he thinks of is what somebody else has entrusted to him.
The second layer: "he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife." He says out loud exactly where that line runs, without the least trace of vagueness.
The third layer, and the deepest of the three: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?"

He does not say, "How can I do such a stupid thing?" He does not say, "I would be found out." He does not even say, "That would be a wrong against my master" — he has already said that part. What he says is "this great wickedness" (הָרָעָה הַגְּדֹלָה, *hara'ah hagedolah*) and "sin against God" (וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים, *vechatati lElohim*).
"To sin" is חָטָא (*chata*) in the Hebrew, and its root sense is to miss the target.

Brothers and sisters, that is the definition of the fear of God: not being afraid of being found out, but being afraid of offending that One — which is precisely why it makes no difference whether anybody is watching.

And there is something else we must notice: this was not a single temptation. Verse 10 says, "As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn't listen to her" — in the Hebrew that is יוֹם יוֹם (*yom yom*), day after day after day.
This was a siege that went on and on. And the text adds one more phrase: "or to be with her." He not only refused to listen; he kept away from the situation altogether.

And then came that day. "About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside. She caught him by his garment, saying, 'Lie with me!' He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside." (Genesis 39:11–12)
"There were none of the men of the house inside" — the most dangerous moment of all is the moment when there is no witness.
And what Joseph did was very simple, and not the least bit heroic: he ran.
"Ran" is וַיָּנָס (*vayyanas*) in the Hebrew. 2 Timothy 2:22 says, "Flee from youthful lusts" — that is exactly the idea Paul is working with.

Some temptations are to be resisted where you stand; others are to be handled by leaving the room. People who cannot tell those two apart very often go down on the words, "I want to prove I can take it."

And notice the verb behind "he left his garment", עָזַב (*azav*) — it is the same word as in verse 6, where the master "left all that he had in Joseph's hand." He would sooner throw away his clothing than throw away that trust.

This is the second time Joseph has been stripped of his clothes. The first time his brothers stripped him; the second time he took it off himself, in order to hold God's boundary. And on both occasions the result was the same — he went further down.
Joseph's refusal has three layers. Which of them is the deepest?

The first layer is "my master trusts me" — the very first thing he thinks of is what somebody else has entrusted to him. The second is "he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife" — he says where the line runs without the least trace of vagueness. The third, and the deepest: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" He does not say, "How can I do such a stupid thing?" He does not say, "I would be found out." And the root sense of the Hebrew word behind "sin" is to miss the target. That is the definition of the fear of God: not being afraid of being found out, but being afraid of offending that One — which is precisely why it makes no difference whether anybody is watching. Whether a person holds the line turns, in the end, not on willpower but on who it is he is afraid of.
Why does he run instead of standing his ground?

Because some temptations are to be resisted where you stand, and others are to be handled by leaving the room. 2 Timothy says, "Flee from youthful lusts", and that is exactly the idea Paul is working with. Two details are worth noticing. Verse 10 says she spoke to Joseph "day by day" — that is a siege that went on and on, not a single temptation; and the text adds "or to be with her", which means he kept away from the situation altogether. A great many people go down on the words, "I want to prove I can take it." The working principle is very simple: a predictable temptation is dealt with by a rule set in advance — do not be alone with that person, do not do it late at night, do not carry on a private exchange of messages.
3. Put into the Prison, and That Sentence Comes Again
What happens next is written very fast, and very coldly.
The woman calls the men of the household first. Listen to how she puts it: "Behold, he has brought a Hebrew in to us to mock us." (Genesis 39:14)

She does not say "Joseph"; she says "a Hebrew." She does not say "the man my husband bought"; she says "he has brought him in to us." In one sentence she draws a line between the races, shifts the responsibility onto her husband, and pulls the servants standing there onto her own side of it — "us."

Then, when the master gets home, the same speech is made a second time with two words changed: "The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought to us, came in to me to mock me." To the servants it was "a Hebrew"; to her husband it is "the Hebrew servant." To the servants it was "he" who brought him in; to her husband it is "you."

Brothers and sisters, a false accusation is a craft. It is never a matter of inventing one enormous lie; it is a matter of putting true things into the right position — and she really did have that garment in her hand.

"When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying, 'This is what your servant did to me,' his wrath was kindled. Joseph's master took him, and put him into the prison." (Genesis 39:19–20)
"His wrath was kindled" is וַיִּחַר אַפּוֹ (*vayyichar appo*) in the Hebrew, and literally it reads, "his nose burned."

Commentators have noticed something here. Under Egyptian law, a slave accused of assaulting the mistress of the house would ordinarily be put to death, not imprisoned. And Potiphar was captain of the guard — the place of execution was under his own authority. If he had genuinely believed every word of it, Joseph would never have lived to reach chapter 40.

The text does not say so outright, and neither shall we say more than it does. All we know is this: the man who did the right thing was shut up in "the place where the king's prisoners were bound." Psalm 105 says, "They bruised his feet with shackles. His neck was locked in irons."
The end of verse 20 gives us one sentence with no feeling in it at all: "and he was there in custody."
And then the first word of verse 21 is the most powerful turn in the whole Bible:
"But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison." (Genesis 39:21)
He was sold, he was falsely accused, he was locked up — but Yahweh was with him.

"Showed kindness to him" is וַיֵּט אֵלָיו חָסֶד (*vayyet elav chesed*), and חֶסֶד (*chesed*) is God's faithful, covenant-keeping love. "Gave him favor" reads, in the original, "granted him his favour" — favour is a thing given, never a thing earned.
Then in verse 23 that sentence appears for the fourth time: "because Yahweh was with him; and that which he did, Yahweh made it prosper."
Word for word the same sentence — one of them spoken in Potiphar's house, the other spoken inside a prison. The text describes those two places in identical language, and it is telling us one thing:
The location changed; God did not. A person who has God inside him will give off the same light whichever place you move him to.
What is worth seeing clearly in the way that woman framed her accusation?

A false accusation is a craft. It is never a matter of inventing one enormous lie; it is a matter of putting true things into the right position — and she really did have that garment in her hand. Then look at her wording. To the servants: "he has brought a Hebrew in to us to mock us" — she draws a line between the races, shifts the responsibility onto her husband, and pulls the people standing there onto her own side of it as "us." To her husband, two words change: "the Hebrew servant, whom you have brought to us." The same incident, with the telling adjusted to the audience. Recognising this craft matters, because the very same technique is being used every day in our group chats and our workplaces; and it warns us about our own speech too — never win by a careful selection of true things.
4. What He Did Inside the Prison

Verse 22 holds a detail that is easily read straight past: "The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever they did there, he was responsible for it."

Count it through from the top of this chapter. Potiphar "put all that he had into his hand"; the keeper of the prison "committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners who were in the prison"; and by chapter 41 Pharaoh says, "Behold, I have set you over all the land of Egypt."
Three times, something is put into his hand. God adds one layer, and then another.

Brothers and sisters, that seventeen-year-old in the coat of many colours, who could do nothing but talk about his dreams, could never have governed Egypt. The man who governed Egypt was the one who learned to keep the accounts in Potiphar's house, learned to handle people inside a prison, and learned in thirteen wrongfully accused years how to keep his mouth shut.
God did not waste those thirteen years. He was making a man.

And notice Joseph's bearing inside that prison. He did not draft a petition. He did not go about protesting his innocence. He did not settle down inside his own self-pity. What he did was this — he did well the thing that was in front of him.
In the next lesson we shall see that the first thing he says in prison to two dejected officials is, "Why do you look so sad today?"
A man who has been wronged, and he is still watching the faces of other people. That is the true stature of this man.
Let me say this very honestly: this chapter does not hand us a formula in which good people get good outcomes. He held the line, and the result was prison. We cannot fudge our way past that.
What the text gives is not a formula. It is one word: but.

Can you put that "but" in front of your own circumstances? I have lost my job, but Yahweh is with me. The diagnosis has come back, but Yahweh is with me. That whole matter was misunderstood and I still have not been able to clear it up, but Yahweh is with me.
That "but" is not a way of comforting yourself. It is a fact this chapter repeats four times over, and tests against two completely opposite sets of circumstances.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
Preached carelessly, this chapter can wound people. There are several places we have to be able to recognise.

The first distortion is preaching God's presence as a guarantee that things will go smoothly. Two of the four "Yahweh was with him" sentences are spoken inside a prison. Preach it as prosperity and the moment your congregation meets trouble they will assume God has walked out. The test is this: when someone who is suffering right now has heard you, does he still believe God is with him?

The second distortion is preaching Joseph's later success as the reward for having kept himself pure. He held the line, and the immediate result was prison — and once he was in, he was in for years. The text gives no formula in which good people get good outcomes. Preach it as a reward, and the people who did the right thing and lost by it will go home disappointed, and may even start wondering whether they were simply not good enough.

The third distortion is preaching running away as cowardice. For certain temptations the Bible's own instruction is to flee. That is courage, not retreat. Get it backwards and somebody in the room will stay in a dangerous situation in order to prove something about himself. What the congregation ought to learn here is to leave the room, not to grit their teeth and hold on.

The fourth distortion is scolding Joseph for not being wise enough, as though that is why he was falsely accused. The text does not reproach him at any point. Pushing the responsibility back onto the victim is a very dangerous way to preach, and it wounds a second time over anybody who has ever been falsely accused. Every single thing he did was right, and he was locked up anyway — that is what the text is asking us to face.

The fifth distortion is preaching prospering at work as a formula for making money. Joseph's prospering was a slave running his master's household well. Not one coin of that prospering went into his own pocket. Preach it as a principle for getting rich and you have turned God into an investment instrument.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we very easily read a run of bad fortune as "God is displeased with me." Our elders will say, "Is there something you didn't do properly?" — and we think along the same lines ourselves: was my giving not enough? Did I offend God somewhere? Brothers and sisters, this chapter cuts that wire. Joseph did the right thing and ended up in prison; two of the four "Yahweh was with him" sentences are spoken inside a jail. Your circumstances are not a dashboard showing how much God loves you. This week, if there is a sentence inside you that runs "maybe God doesn't want me any more", I am asking you to put a "but" in front of that sentence, then write the whole thing down and stick it up somewhere you will see it.

The second question: at work we very often feel, "This isn't where I ought to be, so doing it half-heartedly will do." Our minds are on changing jobs, on ministry, on getting serious once the opportunity finally arrives. But Joseph, in Potiphar's house and in the prison alike, did the thing in front of him as well as it could possibly be done. That Egyptian did not come to see God by listening to Joseph preach the gospel; he saw it by watching him work. Brothers and sisters, the position you occupy right now is your pulpit. This week, let one colleague see something a little different in the quality of your work.
What do you do when you have been falsely accused and there is no way to prove yourself?

From beginning to end this chapter does not record a single word of self-defence from Joseph. It only says that he was put into the prison, and then says once again, "Yahweh was with Joseph." This is not telling anyone to refuse to set the record straight — say what needs saying, keep the evidence that needs keeping, use the channels of appeal that are open to you. What it is saying is this: when you have already done everything you could and the verdict still will not turn, you have not been thrown away. In practice there are three things you can do. First, write down what happened — dates, people, what was said. Second, find one or two people who know the situation to stand as witnesses, and let them know where you are. Third, go on doing well the work that is in your hands — because what finally lifted him up again was precisely the way he went about his work inside that prison.
7. Living 321 Out — Where Nobody Is Watching
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Joseph left his garment behind and ran. And when our Lord was tempted in the wilderness, what he used was "It is written" — and then the devil left him. In the prayer he taught us there is a line that runs, "Bring us not into temptation" — even the prayer the Lord Jesus taught is asking God not to let us walk into the place at all. My role model shows me this: some temptations are not resisted where you stand; they are handled by leaving the room.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "don't get caught"; the standard is "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" Feeling says, "This once, nobody will know." The standard says, "Missing the target is missing the target." When those two collide, listen to the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. A boundary has to be drawn in advance; it cannot be worked out on the spot. On the spot a person relies on his intellect, and to rely on our intellect is to rely on ourselves, which breeds worry — and the moment worry starts, a person starts hunting for reasons. To rely on the heart is to rely on the Holy Spirit, and that brings gladness: in a quiet hour ask the Holy Spirit to give you the boundary, and in the dangerous hour all you have to do is walk the line you were already given.

Let Jesus be King. "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" — the boundary is drawn for God, not for a reputation. To let Jesus be King is for the places nobody sees to come under his rule as well: your phone, your late nights, your hours alone, your business trips. If a king governs only the public occasions, then he is no king at all.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The text says it plainly: it is not that Joseph was capable, it is that "Yahweh made all that he did prosper in his hand." Even that Egyptian master could see it. The time when we are doing well is exactly the time to be most careful that we do not enter that prospering on our own account.

Establish God's system. Potiphar put everything into his hand; the keeper of the prison committed the prisoners to his hand; Pharaoh set him over the whole land. God adds one layer, and then another, making the man for a trust that is still to come. To establish God's system begins with faithfulness in small things — "He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much."
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same "But"
We come to this chapter carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "A temptation like that I can carry." Joseph did not carry it; he ran. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, imagining that we have the strength to stand at the cliff edge and not fall off it. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings, admitting that I am a person who can fall — and therefore I do not go to that place at all. Running is not losing. Running is knowing who you are.

The fearful heart says, "If I do the right thing, won't I be the one who loses out?" You will. That is exactly what happens in this chapter. But brothers and sisters, losing out and being thrown away are two different things. He lost out, and God was there the whole way through. Fear adds up the profit and loss lying in front of it; faith looks at that "but."

The ashamed heart says, "In a situation like that I didn't manage to run, so I am finished." This chapter is not here to condemn you. What you need to look at is Judah — the man who failed utterly in the chapter before this one, and whose name the writer has put into the genealogy of Christ. What the gospel gives is not "you were fine all along." What the gospel gives is "you can start running from today."

The wounded heart says, "I was wronged, and to this day not one person has spoken a word for me." Joseph was wronged for more than a decade, and the text never once records him arguing his own case. In the end God overturned the verdict himself, and overturned it on a scale far larger than anything Joseph could have thought of. You do not have to go and collect justice for yourself. The One who vindicates you is never late.
Four kinds of heart, and one and the same "but." Whichever of those hearts you are sitting in, that sentence stands in front of you: but Yahweh was with him.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Every day, before you start work, before you start school, before you open the shop, pray one sentence: "Lord, this day is done for you." Just that one sentence, for seven days.
Second, towards yourself. Put a "but" in front of the circumstances you are in right now, write that whole sentence down, and stick it up somewhere you will see it.

Third, towards people. Let one colleague, one classmate or one member of your family see something a little different in the quality of your work. You do not have to open your mouth and preach the gospel. Let him see it first.

Fourth, towards daily living. Settle one boundary in advance — which kind of occasion you will not attend, at what hour you will not meet anyone alone, which kind of message you will not answer. Write it down, and tell one companion you trust.
Fifth, towards your calling. In the position you occupy right now, do one very small thing faithfully and well. Just one — done to the point where even you are satisfied with it.

Sixth, tell it in three sentences to one friend outside the church. The first: there is a man in the Bible who was sold as a slave and then falsely accused and put in prison. The second: that chapter says "God was with him" four times over, and every one of those four falls in his very worst days. The third: so I have learned to put a "but" in front of my own hard places.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that God's presence does not depend on my circumstances; wherever I am, he is there.
I declare that my boundary is drawn for God and not for a reputation; the places where nobody sees are under his rule too.
I declare that where I ought to flee, I will flee; leaving the room is not cowardice, it is obedience.
I declare that I will be faithful in the position I am in right now; faithfulness in small things is the way God makes me.
How do you practise this "where nobody is watching"?

Begin in three very small places. First, time: what do you do with that half hour when nobody is checking on you — that is the most honest medical examination there is. Second, your phone: what is it that you open when you are alone at night. Set a boundary that actually works — putting the phone outside the bedroom at a fixed hour, for instance — rather than relying on resolve alone. Third, speech: how you talk about somebody you do not like when he is not in the room. Nobody sees any of those three things, and all three of them slowly grow into the person you are. If you find that one of them has been out of control over a long period, do not grit your teeth alone: find a trustworthy companion of your own sex to ask you about it regularly, and seek professional help where that is needed.
When this chapter opens, Joseph is brought down into Egypt; when this chapter closes, Joseph is shut inside a prison. Seen from a human point of view, he has been going downhill the whole way.

And yet this chapter repeats one and the same sentence four times over. Twice while he wears the status of a slave, twice in the middle of iron chains. It is as though the text were afraid we might not hear, and so it says it, and says it again:

So Jesus is the focal point — not myself, not other people, not my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the God who is "with us" was afterwards given a name, and that name is Immanuel; and he himself was sold, and falsely accused, and sentenced, and stripped of his clothes and hung on a piece of wood. He went all the way down into the deepest prison of all, so that however far we fall, at whatever level we land, we can put that one word in front of our own circumstances — but.

May God bless every one of us to give off light in the position we now occupy; may the boundary you drew in advance still stand when nobody is watching; and may you hear, on the days that feel most like being thrown away, that one sentence: but Yahweh is with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — a lesson that never reaches the third transformation has stopped at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if there is time to spare. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be completed at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ All four occurrences of "Yahweh was with Joseph" fall in slavery and in prison. Why is his presence not the same thing as an easy road?
2. ★★ "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" Is the fear of God being afraid of discovery, or being afraid of offending that One?
3. ★ The master could not see him pray, and yet he could see that Yahweh was with him. How does the quality of a person's work speak on his behalf?
4. ★★ Some temptations are to be resisted where you stand, others are to be handled by leaving the room. How do you tell which is which?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can carry it), fearful (I am afraid of being falsely accused), ashamed (where nobody is watching I cannot hold the line), wounded (I was wronged and nobody spoke for me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "But Yahweh was with Joseph." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something in your hands that nobody sees? What is it that makes you loosen your grip in that particular thing?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The place where I most need a boundary is …"
9. ★★ This week, which workable boundary are you going to set? Say the time, the place and the method; do not just state a resolve.

Leader's reminder: the question about the thing nobody sees will touch private struggles. Anyone at all may answer with nothing more than "I know what that is." Do not press for details; this question is better discussed with the men and the women in separate groups. If someone has been out of control over a long period, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ At home, is there something you will not do unless somebody is watching? Say how you are going to change it.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, which one thing, done well, would speak on your behalf?
12. ★★★ The practice of working well: this week, take the one task in your hands you least want to do, and do it as well as it can be done. Say which one it is.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to check with you once a week, at a set time, on how the boundary is holding. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson in three sentences to one friend outside the church. The first: there is a slave in the Bible whose master's wife pestered him day after day; he left his clothing behind and ran, and for that he was falsely accused and put in prison. The second: the reason he gave was not "I would be found out" but "How can I sin against God?" The third: so what I have learned is that a person's bottom line is grown in the hours when nobody is watching. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one boundary you are going to set, and the one task you are going to do as well as it can be done. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that in the places where nobody is watching, we may still know that there is One who sees.
